strengths: The paper makes a genuine conceptual contribution by organizing the expressivity analysis of weight-space networks into four well-motivated approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators), each tied to real-world applications (Figure 2). This taxonomy is useful for future work and clarifies why expressivity analysis in weight-space learning is subtler than in other GDL settings.

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2 / Theorem D.6) is clean and practically relevant: proving that DWS, NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN are mutually approximable via an explicit cycle of constructive simulations (Appendix D.4) unifies a diverse body of prior work and legitimately allows the rest of the analysis to use a single representative architecture. The NFT case (Propositions D.21, D.22) is handled carefully, including a concrete separation construction and a GP-based recovery of equivalence.

The universality results under general position (Theorems 6.3, 7.4) are proved constructively via a canonization map based on sorting distinct bias values, and the accompanying impossibility results (Propositions 6.2, 7.3) are based on a concrete WL-indistinguishable pair with different matrix ranks. Together with the supporting hierarchy of equivalence relations (Theorem E.4: G < DWS < functional equivalence), this gives a coherent and fairly complete picture for the invariant/equivariant operator settings.

The analysis of function-space operators is the most novel part: the negative result (Theorem F.9) uses bounded geometric complexity (number of linearity regions and vertices, Lemma F.12) and closure of piecewise-affine classes (Lemma F.13) to show fixed-architecture weight-to-weight maps cannot increase complexity, while Theorem F.10 shows universality is recovered when the input architecture is allowed to grow, via a partition-of-unity lifting. This yields a non-trivial and practically relevant insight connecting overparameterization to weight-space expressivity.

The manuscript is honest about limitations: it explicitly excludes scale-equivariant architectures, discusses low-precision regimes where the exclusion-set assumption fails, notes that empirical validation of the capacity prediction is open, and admits (Appendix E.3 remark) that the main-text proof sketch of Theorem 6.3 is intuition-building rather than the formal proof.
weaknesses: The paper's central universality machinery relies heavily on recent, apparently unrefereed arXiv preprints: Theorem 6.1/E.9 invokes a separation-to-approximation theorem from [50] (Theorem 1) and the proof of Theorem 6.1 also builds on [51], and the NFT equivalence (Proposition D.22) leans on 'update primitives' from the authors' own proof of Theorem 7.4 plus Lim et al. [41, Proposition 10]. The correctness of several headline claims is therefore contingent on external results that the community has not yet vetted; a more self-contained treatment (at least of the key separation-to-approximation step) would substantially strengthen the paper.

The results are exclusively asymptotic/existential with no quantitative content: no approximation rates, no bounds on required network size/depth, and Theorem F.10 is qualitative ('there exists δ and an architecture A'), which limits its practical guidance despite the paper's claims of 'principled guidance' for architecture design.

Scope is narrower than the abstract's 'comprehensive characterization' framing suggests: only MLP weight spaces, only hidden-neuron permutation symmetry (scale/sign equivariance explicitly excluded), ReLU-specific negative results for function-space operators (with only a conjectured extension to other activations), and continuous targets on compact sets. The broad framing somewhat overstates the reach of the theorems.

There are presentation inconsistencies that could mislead readers: the main-text proof sketch of Theorem 6.3 (canonization + argsort argument) is not the argument actually used in the formal proof (Appendix E.3 reduces to Theorem 7.4 instead); several definitions in Appendix D are heavy and dense (e.g., the GMN/NG feature constructions), making verification laborious; and the main text states Proposition 7.1 only 'informally' with the formal statement deferred entirely to the appendix.

No empirical component whatsoever. While acceptable for a theory paper, several of the paper's own practical predictions (e.g., that larger input architectures unlock function-space operator capabilities, that simplified DWS subsets suffice) remain unvalidated, and the limitation section correctly flags this; even a small sanity-check experiment simulating the canonization-based constructions would have increased confidence.

Several proof steps in Appendix F warrant closer scrutiny: Lemma F.4's use of DeepSets universality to approximate the locally-constant ranking map relies on the ranking being continuous on K, which holds only because K avoids E, and the interplay between approximation of NI and the exact lexicographic sorting in cannon (Lemma F.7) involves tolerance choices (epsilon-chains through multiple MLP approximations, Eq. 189-197) whose cumulative error propagation is asserted rather than rigorously tracked.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior expressivity results for weight-space networks ([34, 41, 49]) are capability-specific (forward-pass simulation, subsumption) rather than general approximation guarantees, and this submission provides the first systematic, unified treatment across four carefully motivated approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators), with real-world examples grounding each setting (Figure 2).

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2) is a useful unification: proving that DWS, NP-NFN, HNP-NFN, GMN, and NG-GNN are mutually approximable on compact sets, with a precise characterization of where NFTs differ and how the gap closes under general position (Proposition 5.3, Propositions D.21–D.22). The cyclic containment proof (D.4) is detailed and largely constructive, with explicit layer-by-layer constructions.

The negative results are arguably the most valuable contributions: Proposition 6.2/7.3 identify concrete orbit-separation obstructions (rank-based counterexample distinguishable by G-orbits but not by WL-equivalent neural graphs), and Theorem F.9 gives a clean geometric-complexity argument (bounded linear regions, closedness of PL_{M,R}) explaining why fixed-architecture weight-to-weight maps cannot realize complexity-increasing function-space operators such as zoom-out transformations.

The topological groundwork is careful: continuity of the realization map and the equivalence of supremum and quotient topologies on compact weight sets (Appendix C) correctly justify the passage between function-space and weight-space continuity, which is the subtle point the abstract rightly flags.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific (no optimization/generalization analysis, low-precision regimes violating GP, scale-equivariant networks and non-MLP architectures out of scope, unvalidated prediction about growing architectures).
weaknesses: The paper is entirely theoretical with no empirical component whatsoever. Given that the paper's own motivation is practical ('principled guidance on when existing architectures suffice'), even a small experiment (e.g., verifying that DWS/GMN/NG-GNN/NFT indeed behave equivalently on representative tasks, or illustrating the fixed-architecture operator limitation of Theorem F.9 on INR editing) would substantially strengthen the claims. As written, Figure 1's practical implications rest purely on approximation-theoretic arguments.

Several headline results are heavily assembled from prior work rather than new machinery: Theorem 6.1 leans on Navon et al.'s forward-pass simulation plus the separation-to-approximation theorem of Pacini et al. [51]; the NFT containment direction of Proposition 5.3 relies on Lim et al. [41, Proposition 10]; and the GP-universality pattern (canonization via sorting a discriminating feature, universality outside a measure-zero exclusion set) is a well-established template in GDL ([43, 44, 16]). The novelty is in the careful adaptation to weight space, which is real but incremental.

The general-position assumption deserves more scrutiny. The exclusion set is defined by pairwise-distinct biases per layer, and the paper claims such configurations 'are unlikely to arise under random initialization or stochastic training dynamics.' This is contestable: zero or constant bias initialization is extremely common in practice, and trained networks frequently exhibit near-degenerate biases. The discussion of quantization in Section 6.2 acknowledges the issue only obliquely; the practical reach of the universality theorems is therefore narrower than the framing suggests.

Theorem 7.2 is stated informally in the main text, and its formal counterpart (Theorem F.10) involves a somewhat delicate quantifier structure: the architecture A is chosen after the target set K, and the guarantee holds only on a δ-approximating set K′ rather than on realized-function sets directly. The main-text statement ('sufficiently large architecture A and any compact set K′ ⊂ V\E whose realized functions approximate those in K') does not make fully clear that A and K′ must be chosen jointly with δ, which risks readers over-interpreting the result.

There are presentation-order dependencies that complicate verification: the formal proof of Theorem 6.3 (E.11) is derived from Theorem 7.4 proved later, and Proposition D.22 depends on Theorems 7.4 and 6.3; the appendix itself acknowledges that the proof sketch in Section 6.2 'is conceptually different' from the formal argument actually used. The intuition-building sketch (canonization via DeepSets-approximated ranking) is thus not the argument of record, which is confusing for a reader trying to verify the central universality claims.

Equivalence of expressive power in the sense of Definition 5.1/D.3 compares closures of architecture classes on compact sets; this is coarse. It does not distinguish depth, width, or parameter efficiency — architectures deemed 'equally expressive' may require drastically different sizes to achieve the same approximation error, which limits the practical guidance the paper claims to offer. A remark on this would help.

The negative result of Proposition 6.2 and the hierarchy result (Theorem E.4) rest on a single hand-constructed counterexample family; the WL-indistinguishability argument in Proposition E.8 is asserted via 'a direct computation' with reference to a figure, and an explicit verification would improve confidence.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and clearly stated gap: prior expressivity results for weight-space networks (Navon et al., Lim et al., Kalogeropoulos et al.) are partial/simulation-based, and this paper delivers the first comprehensive characterization covering both weight-space and function-space approximation targets.

The four-setting approximation framework (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) is a clean conceptual contribution that organizes what 'expressivity' means in weight-space learning, with convincing real-world motivation for each setting (Figure 2).

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2, Appendix D) is thorough: a full cyclic containment proof (DWS ↔ NP-NFN+PE ↔ GMN ↔ NG ↔ DWS) with explicit, careful constructions, including the interesting finding that NFTs are the sole exception, resolved exactly under a general-position assumption (Proposition 5.3).

The universality results are well-motivated and the exclusion-set (general position) framing is natural and honest: the paper proves universality under the mild distinct-bias assumption and, importantly, also proves the complement — where universality fails (Propositions 6.2, 7.3, 7.1/Theorem F.9) — via concrete WL-indistinguishability and linear-region arguments. The identification of the fixed-architecture obstruction for function-space operators (Theorem F.9) with the zoom-out operator example is an insightful, novel limitation analysis.

Supporting topological machinery (continuity of the realization map, equivalence of sup-norm and quotient topologies on compact weight sets, canonization map via bias sorting) is developed carefully and reused consistently across proofs.

Honest limitations discussion: explicitly notes results are expressivity-only (no optimization/generalization claims), that the capacity prediction of Theorem 7.2 is unvalidated empirically, that low-precision regimes may violate the GP assumption, and that scale-equivariant and CNN/Transformer settings are out of scope.

Extensive, detailed appendices (approx. 47 pages of proofs) that restate results, formalize network definitions, and make the constructions verifiable; the reduction of Theorem 6.3 to Theorem 7.4 in Appendix E.3 is transparently flagged as differing from the main-text sketch.
weaknesses: Purely theoretical with no experiments at all; the practically most interesting prediction — that sufficiently large input architectures unlock function-space operators (Theorem 7.2) — remains empirically unvalidated, and the paper acknowledges this. No reconstruction/accuracy experiments even on toy function-space operators.

No quantitative bounds: all results are existence/universality statements without depth, width, or sample complexity of the approximating networks. The constructions (e.g., canonization via sorting, finite-index MLP banks in Lemma F.7) plausibly require very large networks, so the practical import of 'universality' is hard to gauge.

Some individual proof components lean heavily on prior work: the equivalence cycle partially reuses Lim et al. [41, Prop. 10], Lemma D.13 restates Lim et al. [40, Lemma 6], and Theorem 6.1 relies on Pacini et al. [50, 51]. The novelty is in assembling the complete cycle and characterization rather than in each individual technique.

The negative results (Propositions 6.2, 7.3) are somewhat expected given known GNN/WL and exclusion-set phenomena in GDL; their value is in transferring them to the weight-space setting rather than conceptual surprise.

The main-text Theorems 7.2 and Proposition 7.1 are only informally stated, and the formal versions (Appendix F.2, Theorems F.9/F.10) carry important qualifiers (fixed ReLU architecture, compact K', δ-approximation, architecture chosen relative to the target operator) that a reader of the main text could miss.
Appendix D.22 explicitly relies on results proven later in the appendix (Theorem 7.4), creating circular presentation ordering that, while acknowledged, complicates verification.

Minor presentation issues: occasional typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'proposition 6.3' reference, informal vs. formal statement mismatch of Proposition 7.3/7.1 labeling), and the scope is confined to MLP weight spaces with hidden-neuron permutation symmetry, excluding scale-equivariant and other architectures (acknowledged in footnote and limitations).

strengths: Comprehensive and systematic contribution: the paper unifies prior partial expressivity results (Navon et al. 2023; Lim et al. 2023; Kalogeropoulos et al. 2024) into a single framework, proving that DWS, NFN (both variants), GMN, and NG-GNN are expressively equivalent, with NFT joining under a natural general-position assumption (Theorem 5.2, Proposition 5.3). This settles an open, actively discussed question in the weight-space learning literature.

The four-setting approximation framework (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) is well motivated by real tasks (Figure 2) and yields a clean, complete characterization: universality holds under GP (Theorems 6.1, 6.3, 7.4) and fails in identifiable edge-case regimes (Propositions 6.2, 7.1). The hierarchy of equivalence relations in Theorem E.4 (G-equivariance strictly stronger than DWS-indistinguishability, which is strictly stronger than functional equivalence) is a genuinely insightful structural result.

The proofs are careful and substantive: ~55 pages of appendix include explicit constructions (canonization maps, neuron-identification maps, cycle of expressive containments D.17–D.20, formal simulation of GMN by NG layers), a rigorous topological treatment of the realization map (Appendix C), and a non-universality argument via bounded geometric complexity of fixed ReLU architectures (Lemma F.12, closedness in F.13).

Theory is connected to practice in two credible ways: (i) empirical validation of the general-position assumption on 60k pretrained MNIST INRs, including a quantization study showing GP collapse at low bit precision (Appendix G.1), and (ii) Output Capacity Expansion (OCE), a simple, theory-driven modification whose gains (up to 34% over prior SOTA on MNIST INR dilation) are obtained under a controlled parameter budget, ruling out a trivial 'more parameters' explanation (Appendix I.1, Table 2).

The paper is honest about scope: limitations (no optimization/generalization theory, reliance on expressivity only, exclusion-set choice, ReLU-specific operator limitation) are explicitly discussed, and extensions to transformer weight spaces and alternative exclusion sets (p-norms) strengthen generality.
Good presentation: the expressivity landscape figure, proof sketches in the main text, and a consistent formal framework make the dense material accessible.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is limited to a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation). The 34% SOTA claim rests on one task; additional operator-editing tasks (e.g., other INR benchmarks such as MNIST classification or super-resolution used in prior work) would substantially strengthen the practical claim.

Several key proofs lean heavily on results from very recent or concurrent work: Theorem 6.1 invokes the separation-to-approximation theorem of Pacini et al. (2025b,a) as a black box, and Proposition D.18 relies on Lim et al. (2023, Proposition 10). The novelty of the contribution partly depends on these external tools; the paper would benefit from more self-contained statements of the exact assumptions under which these apply.

A minor but noticeable inconsistency: Proposition D.22's proof of NFT equivalence uses multi-headed attention ('we use multi-headed attention to simultaneously compute...') while the formal Definition D.12 is single-head; the paper acknowledges multi-head in a remark but the proof should be made consistent with the stated definition.

The non-universality result for function-space operators (Proposition 7.1 / Theorem F.9) is limited to ReLU activations, and the authors only conjecture adaptability to other nonlinearities; also the practical bite of the fixed-architecture limitation is demonstrated only indirectly via the OCE experiment.

Universality results are existence/approximation results on compact sets; no constructive bounds on required network size are given, and the gap between the measure-zero exclusion set and worst-case behavior (relevant for quantized weights, as the authors themselves note) means the GP assumption is necessary rather than fully benign — the practical follow-through (e.g., architectures robust on E) is deferred to future work.

The claimed 'comprehensive characterization' is scoped to permutation equivariance on MLP weights; scale-equivariant networks (ScaleGMN etc.) and other symmetry groups are excluded, which is reasonable but slightly weakens the breadth implied by the abstract.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely open question in weight-space learning and organizes it into a clear framework: the four approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) are a useful conceptual contribution that future work can build on.

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2, with NFT as an exception resolved under general position) unifies a scattered literature and is a clean, useful clarification, supported by detailed constructions in a ~55-page appendix.

The negative result that function-space operators cannot be approximated by fixed-architecture weight-to-weight maps (Proposition 7.1 / Theorem F.9) is a meaningful limitation result, and the proof via bounded piecewise-affine complexity is sound and well-motivated.

The theory-to-practice link is a strength: OCE is directly motivated by Theorem 7.2, and the ablation over ensemble size (Table 2) shows monotone improvement consistent with the theory, with parameter counts controlled to avoid trivially larger-model explanations.

The treatment of the general-position assumption is unusually careful: multiple admissible exclusion sets are characterized (Appendix G), and the empirical validation of GP rates under quantization is an honest and informative addition.
weaknesses: Much of the technical content assembles existing results rather than introducing new machinery: the equivalence proofs lean on Lim et al. (2023, Prop. 10) and the DWS basis characterization of Navon et al. (2023); Theorem 6.1 relies centrally on the separation-to-approximation theorem of Pacini et al. (2025b, an arXiv preprint); and the canonization-by-bias-sorting proof technique closely follows well-established universality arguments (Maron et al., 2019/2020; Segol & Lipman, 2019). The genuinely new results (hierarchy of equivalence relations, operator settings) are valuable but the overall novelty is moderate.

Several main results are fairly expected: it is unsurprising that these architectures, all encoding the same symmetry group, are expressively equivalent, and the fixed-architecture operator limitation (bounded linear regions) is close to a folklore observation. The paper's headline framing ('comprehensive characterization') somewhat oversells the surprise value of the findings.

Theorem 7.2 is stated only informally in the main text and its 'sufficiently large architecture' condition is non-constructive; the connection between this abstract theorem and the concrete OCE modification (which keeps the input architecture fixed and only increases the output feature dimension) is loose, weakening the claim that the empirical gains validate the theory specifically.

The empirical evaluation is thin for the significance claimed: a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation), two base architectures, and only 3 seeds. OCE is essentially output ensembling with averaging, a well-known technique, and the paper does not disentangle the benefit of ensembling per se from the theory-motivated capacity increase (e.g., no comparison to naive weight-space ensembling baselines or other capacity-matched alternatives).

The SOTA claim relies on baseline numbers taken verbatim from prior publications under potentially different training setups (hardware, epochs, hyperparameters), rather than re-running competing methods under a controlled protocol; only the k=1 DWS/GMN baselines are reproduced from one source (Gelberg et al., 2026, which involves overlapping authors).
Reproducibility is weakened: the code availability URL is blank in the manuscript ('Code available at .'), so the promised artifact cannot currently be verified.

The scope is restricted to MLP weight spaces and excludes scale-equivariant networks (ScaleGMN, which is the strongest published family on this benchmark), which somewhat narrows the 'comprehensive' claim; the transformer extension (Appendix H) is sketched only at a high level and unvalidated empirically.

There are minor but noticeable presentation/proof-hygiene issues, e.g., informal statements of Theorems 7.1-7.2 in the main text, reliance in Proposition 5.3's proof on results proven much later in the appendix (acknowledged by the authors), and occasional hand-waved steps ('a direct computation shows...').

strengths: Comprehensive and well-organized expressivity framework: the paper identifies four natural approximation settings (function-space functionals, permutation-invariant functionals, function-space operators, permutation-equivariant operators) and gives a systematic treatment of each, which usefully organizes an otherwise fragmented literature.

The architectural equivalence result (Theorem 5.2, with the NFT case handled via Proposition 5.3 under general position) is a valuable unification of DWS, NFN, GMN, NG-GNN, and NFT, and is supported by detailed constructive proofs in Appendix D.

The hierarchy of equivalence relations (Theorem E.4: ~G ⊊ ~DWS ⊊ ~func) provides genuine new understanding of what invariant weight-space networks can and cannot distinguish, including concrete counterexamples (Propositions E.7, E.8).

The function-space operator analysis (Proposition 7.1 / Theorem F.9 and Theorem 7.2) is the most original part: it identifies a fundamental limitation of fixed-architecture weight-to-weight maps (bounded linearity regions) and shows universality is recovered with sufficiently large output architectures — an actionable theoretical insight.

The theory is connected to practice via OCE, which improves over prior SOTA on the MNIST INR dilation benchmark with parameter-matched baselines (Table 2 ablation controls for model size), and the GP assumption is empirically validated on real pretrained INRs, including the interesting quantization analysis (Appendix G).

Thorough supporting material: ~60 pages of appendices, extension to transformer weight spaces (Appendix H), alternative exclusion sets (Appendix G), and explicit code availability support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is thin relative to the theoretical scope: a single benchmark (MNIST INR dilation), two base architectures, and a simple ensemble-averaging modification. The connection between Theorem 7.2 (larger output architecture) and OCE (ensemble of k same-architecture networks with averaging) is heuristic rather than a direct instantiation of the theorem.

Much of the technical machinery adapts existing tools: canonization-based universality under measure-zero exclusion sets follows the established pattern of Maron et al. (2020), Finkelshtein et al. (2025), and Gelberg et al. (2026), and the function-space functional result builds directly on Navon et al. (2023) and Pacini et al. (2025a/b) via the separation-to-approximation lemma. The novelty is in unification and application rather than fundamentally new techniques.

The function-space operator impossibility result (Theorem F.9) is restricted to ReLU activations, and the general claim (Proposition 7.1) is only stated informally in the main text; the paper acknowledges but does not resolve extension to other activations.

Universality statements are approximation-only (existence results on compact sets) and say nothing about optimization difficulty, generalization, or the depth/width required — limitations the authors honestly acknowledge, but which temper the practical guidance value of the theory.

The exposition in the main text is dense and leans heavily on appendix references for formal statements (e.g., Proposition 7.1, Theorems 7.2/F.9/F.10), which may impede readability and verification for the general audience.

Several key supporting results are cited from very recent or concurrent preprints (e.g., Pacini et al., 2025a,b; Gelberg et al., 2026), on which the core universality arguments depend, slightly reducing self-containedness.
